query: Why does time dilate near a black hole?

scene.title: Gravitational Time Dilation
scene.subtitle: Why time flows slower near massive objects

answer.headline: Time dilates near a black hole because intense gravity warps the structure of spacetime, causing clocks deep within a gravitational potential to tick slower relative to observers further away.
body: General relativity posits that space and time are fused into a single four-dimensional fabric called spacetime. Massive objects, such as black holes, do not just sit within this fabric; they warp and curve it. This geometry dictates how objects move and how time progresses, meaning gravity is not merely a force, but a distortion of the spacetime manifold itself.

Gravity is physically equivalent to acceleration. When you are closer to a massive object, you are deeper within a gravitational potential well. Because the speed of light must remain constant for all observers, the universe compensates for this intense curvature by adjusting the rate of time. An observer far away, where the potential is weaker, will see your clock as ticking slower compared to their own.

Consider your four-dimensional motion through the universe as being subject to a universal speed limit—the speed of light. If you are 'stationary' relative to a black hole, you are actually moving entirely through time. However, the extreme curvature of spacetime forces your motion to shift. A portion of your 'velocity' that would normally move you through time is redirected, effectively slowing your passage through the temporal dimension relative to external frames.

This effect intensifies as you move closer to the event horizon. At the horizon, the dilation becomes extreme from the perspective of an outside observer. To someone watching from far away, light coming from an object falling toward the horizon would be infinitely redshifted, and the object's clock would appear to freeze entirely, as the coordinate time stretches toward infinity.
caveats: This explanation assumes general relativity is the accurate model for gravity at these scales.
The distinction between proper time (local to the clock) and coordinate time (observed from a distance) is essential.
